etymologies.heading: Etymology
paragraphs: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1574; borrowed from Latin inveterātus (“of long standing, chronic”), perfect passive participle of inveterō and participial adjective (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, into”) + veterō (“to age”), from vetus, veteris (“old”). Cognate with Italian inveterato, French invétéré. By surface analysis, in- (“not, opposite”) +‎ veterate.
senses: Firmly established from having been around for a long time; of long standing.
(obsolete) To fix and settle after a long time; to entrench.
